title: El Niño Just Crossed the Drought Threshold. India's Monsoon Is Already 18% Short.
excerpt: Sea surface temperatures hit +0.81°C — just above the El Niño line. IMD has downgraded the monsoon forecast to 90% of normal. For 800 million Indians who depend on rain-fed agriculture, the timing could not be worse.
body:
The number that matters is 0.81°C.

As of June 7, sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region — the stretch of equatorial Pacific that climate scientists watch to diagnose El Niño — crossed the +0.80°C threshold. Australia's Bureau of Meteorology confirmed it in their latest Southern Hemisphere Monitoring report. It is a thin margin, but it is the line.

El Niño is not yet officially declared — that requires sustained warming across five overlapping three-month periods. But the trajectory is unmistakable. NOAA and the World Meteorological Organisation both project an 80% chance that El Niño forms between June and August, and a 90% chance it persists into late 2026. Some forecast models suggest this could be the strongest El Niño on record.

For India, the timing is brutal.

**The monsoon is already struggling.** The southwest monsoon arrived in Kerala on June 4 — three days late. It has since advanced into Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, with Kerala's coast receiving up to 280mm of rain in a single 72-hour window. But the national picture is less encouraging. The monsoon is currently running 18% below the long-period average, and the India Meteorological Department has already downgraded its seasonal forecast to 90% of normal rainfall.

IMD Director General Dr. Mrutyunjay Mohapatra has warned that El Niño is likely to emerge in June and gradually intensify through July and August before reaching full strength in September — precisely the months when India's kharif crop planting depends on consistent, well-distributed rainfall.

**What El Niño does to India.** In simple terms, El Niño disrupts the flow of moist winds from the Indian Ocean toward the subcontinent. Historically, El Niño years have meant either late monsoon arrivals, deficient total rainfall, or prolonged dry spells that devastate rain-fed crops.

India's agriculture is extraordinarily exposed. Nearly half the country's farmland lacks irrigation and depends entirely on monsoon rains. The crops most at risk — rice, pulses, oilseeds, and coarse cereals — are also the ones that feed the most people and employ the most farmers.

In the last major El Niño event of 2023, which persisted for 11 months, paddy and pulse production fell significantly, contributing to food inflation that took over a year to subside. That El Niño also helped make 2024 the warmest year on record.

**A potential lifeline from the Indian Ocean.** Not everything points to catastrophe. The Indian Ocean Dipole — a separate climate oscillation — could turn positive during August-September, according to the Bureau of Meteorology. A positive IOD tends to bring additional moisture toward India, and in past El Niño years, it has partially offset the Pacific's drying effect.

But the IOD is currently neutral, with an index value of -0.34°C. Whether it strengthens in time to matter is uncertain. Forecasts suggest neutral conditions will persist through at least June and July.

**The economic stakes are stacking up.** India is already absorbing the costs of the Iran war — oil prices 30% higher than pre-war levels, a 53% spike in the oil-and-gas import bill in April, inflation forecast at 5.1%, and GDP growth projections cut from 7.7% to 6.6%. The RBI is holding rates for now but markets are pricing in hikes.

A weak monsoon would add food inflation to the mix. Farmers in central and peninsular India may delay sowing or shift to less water-intensive crops. Pulses and oilseeds, already volatile, could see tighter supply and higher prices. Rural consumption — the backbone of India's domestic demand story — would take a hit.

Maharashtra's state government has already warned farmers against premature sowing, noting that current pre-monsoon showers are insufficient for crop survival. The monsoon is not expected to reach Delhi until June 25-30.

**For the diaspora, the monsoon is not abstract.** It determines whether your family's farm in Andhra or Rajasthan has a productive season. It shapes food prices for relatives living on fixed incomes. It drives the cost of the groceries, pulses, and rice that stock kitchens from Hyderabad to Houston.

The Pacific is warming. The monsoon is late and light. And India's economic buffers are thinner than they have been in years. What happens in the Niño 3.4 region over the next eight weeks will determine whether India's 2026 turns difficult — or devastating.

*Sources: Australia Bureau of Meteorology, The Hindu BusinessLine, IMD, NOAA, WMO*
